title: Pathophysiology: Respiratory Gas Exchange—Ventilation, V/Q Mismatch and Respiratory Failure
html:
Respiratory function depends on more than an oxygen-saturation number. Air must move to and from functioning alveoli, pulmonary blood must reach those alveoli, gases must cross the alveolar–capillary membrane, hemoglobin must carry oxygen, and circulation must deliver it to tissues. The RN links breathing pattern and effort with oxygen delivery, mental status, perfusion, blood gases, waveform quality, disease mechanism, and response to treatment.

Learning goals

  • Distinguish ventilation, oxygenation, diffusion, perfusion, and tissue oxygen delivery.
  • Relate respiratory rate, tidal volume, dead space, and alveolar ventilation.
  • Explain airway resistance, lung compliance, surfactant, and work of breathing.
  • Compare low V/Q, high V/Q, shunt, and dead-space physiology.
  • Organize the major mechanisms of hypoxemia and hypercapnia.
  • Differentiate hypoxemic and hypercapnic respiratory failure.
  • Recognize respiratory muscle fatigue and impending arrest before apnea occurs.
  • Evaluate oxygen and ventilatory support by clinical response and potential harm.

Ventilation moves carbon dioxide; oxygenation is a different function

Minute ventilation equals respiratory rate multiplied by tidal volume. Only the portion of each breath reaching perfused gas-exchanging alveoli contributes effectively. Alveolar ventilation can be conceptualized as respiratory rate multiplied by tidal volume minus dead-space volume.

A client may breathe rapidly yet ventilate poorly if breaths are very shallow or much of each breath ventilates dead space. Conversely, an apparently normal respiratory rate does not guarantee adequate tidal volume. When alveolar ventilation is inadequate relative to carbon-dioxide production, PaCO₂ rises. Supplemental oxygen can improve oxygenation while carbon dioxide continues to accumulate, so SpO₂ alone cannot establish adequate ventilation.

Oxygenation describes adding oxygen to blood. Ventilation describes movement of air and elimination of carbon dioxide. Respiration also depends on diffusion and cellular use. Always identify which step is failing rather than using these terms interchangeably.

Do not be reassured by one monitor
A client receiving oxygen may show an acceptable SpO₂ while becoming somnolent from worsening hypoventilation and hypercapnia. Assess respiratory effort and depth, mental status, airway, breath sounds, capnography when used, and blood gases when indicated.

Airflow depends on pressure, resistance, and compliance

Air moves down a pressure gradient created by respiratory muscles and changes in thoracic volume. Airway resistance rises sharply as airway radius narrows. Bronchospasm, mucosal edema, secretions, a foreign body, or dynamic airway collapse can therefore markedly limit flow. Turbulence and obstruction increase the effort required to move air.

Compliance describes how readily the lungs and chest wall expand. Low compliance makes inflation difficult, as with pulmonary edema, acute respiratory distress syndrome, fibrosis, or severe atelectasis. Excessively high compliance, as in emphysematous loss of elastic recoil, may make inhalation easier but impair effective exhalation and promote air trapping.

Surfactant lowers alveolar surface tension and helps prevent collapse. Loss or inactivation of surfactant raises opening pressure, reduces compliance, and contributes to atelectasis. Functional residual capacity helps keep alveoli open between breaths and supports an oxygen reservoir.

Work of breathing can become unsustainable

Increased resistance, low compliance, pain, obesity, chest-wall restriction, neuromuscular weakness, fever, acidosis, and high ventilatory demand can all increase respiratory workload. Early compensation may include tachypnea, accessory-muscle use, nasal flaring, retractions, tripod positioning, and diaphoresis.

As fatigue develops, tidal volume may fall, breathing can become irregular, air movement may diminish, PaCO₂ may rise, and mental status may worsen. A falling respiratory rate in a previously distressed client can represent exhaustion rather than improvement. A quiet chest in severe obstructive disease may mean critically limited airflow rather than recovery.

Ventilation and perfusion must meet in the same alveolus

Ventilation (V) is airflow to alveoli; perfusion (Q) is blood flow through adjacent pulmonary capillaries. Regional matching is never perfectly uniform, but disease can produce clinically important extremes.

  • Low V/Q: perfusion exceeds ventilation. Airway obstruction, mucus, pneumonia, edema, or partial alveolar collapse may create this pattern. Oxygen often improves hypoxemia when some ventilation remains.
  • Shunt: perfusion reaches alveoli that receive no ventilation, or blood bypasses ventilated alveoli anatomically. Increasing inspired oxygen may have limited effect when a large true shunt is present because oxygen never reaches the shunted blood.
  • High V/Q: ventilation exceeds perfusion. Pulmonary vascular obstruction or reduced regional blood flow produces wasted ventilation.
  • Dead space: alveoli are ventilated but receive little or no effective perfusion. Pulmonary embolism, very low cardiac output, and overdistended alveoli can increase alveolar dead space.

A client can have several mechanisms simultaneously. For example, ARDS can produce shunt, diffusion impairment, low compliance, and increased dead space; COPD can combine obstruction, air trapping, diffusion loss, and V/Q mismatch.

Diffusion crosses a thin alveolar–capillary barrier

Gas transfer improves with greater surface area and a stronger partial-pressure gradient and worsens as membrane thickness increases. Fibrosis and interstitial or alveolar fluid increase diffusion distance. Emphysema destroys surface area. Oxygen is affected earlier than carbon dioxide in many diffusion disorders because carbon dioxide diffuses more readily.

The alveolar–arterial oxygen gradient can help distinguish reduced inspired oxygen or pure hypoventilation from intrapulmonary V/Q mismatch, shunt, or diffusion limitation. Interpretation depends on inspired oxygen, atmospheric pressure, age, and the clinical context; it is not a stand-alone diagnosis.

Hypoxemia and tissue hypoxia are related but not identical

Hypoxemia is abnormally low oxygen in arterial blood. Major mechanisms include reduced inspired oxygen, hypoventilation, V/Q mismatch, shunt, and diffusion limitation. Hypoxia means inadequate oxygen availability or use at tissues and can result from hypoxemia, anemia, low cardiac output, impaired regional blood flow, or inability of cells to use oxygen.

Most oxygen is carried bound to hemoglobin; only a small portion is dissolved and represented by PaO₂. A client with severe anemia may have an acceptable PaO₂ and SpO₂ but reduced arterial oxygen content. Tissue delivery also depends on cardiac output. For this reason, pulse oximetry must be interpreted with hemoglobin, perfusion, symptoms, and the overall clinical picture.

Pulse oximetry estimates hemoglobin saturation and can be distorted by poor perfusion, motion, nail products, ambient light, probe position, dyshemoglobins, and device limitations across skin pigmentation. Validate an unexpected number, but never delay care when the client is visibly deteriorating.

Hemoglobin affinity changes oxygen loading and unloading

The oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve relates PaO₂ to hemoglobin saturation. Acidemia, higher temperature, and increased carbon dioxide tend to shift the curve to the right, reducing affinity and promoting oxygen unloading to tissues. Alkalemia, lower temperature, and lower carbon dioxide tend to shift it left, increasing affinity and making unloading less ready.

A saturation near the flatter upper portion can change little despite a meaningful PaO₂ change. Once the curve reaches its steeper portion, a modest PaO₂ decline can produce a larger saturation fall. Trends and clinical context matter more than memorizing one cutoff.

Hypercapnia reflects ineffective alveolar ventilation

Carbon dioxide production rises with fever, seizure, increased metabolic activity, and excessive carbohydrate delivery, but the lungs usually compensate by increasing ventilation. Hypercapnia develops when effective alveolar ventilation cannot match production. Causes include depressed respiratory drive, airway obstruction, neuromuscular weakness, chest-wall restriction, severe fatigue, excess dead space, or inadequate mechanical support.

Acute CO₂ retention lowers pH because renal compensation has not yet developed. Chronic retention allows increased renal bicarbonate conservation and a pH closer to baseline. A new pH decline with elevated PaCO₂ and elevated bicarbonate can indicate acute-on-chronic ventilatory failure.

Possible findings include headache, flushed skin, confusion, somnolence, tremor, asterixis, dysrhythmia, and decreasing consciousness. Findings are not specific, so pair them with ventilation assessment and blood-gas data.

Respiratory failure may be hypoxemic, hypercapnic, or mixed

Hypoxemic respiratory failure primarily reflects failure to oxygenate, often from V/Q mismatch, shunt, diffusion impairment, or severe alveolar disease. PaCO₂ may be normal or low initially because compensatory ventilation continues. Hypercapnic respiratory failure reflects inadequate carbon-dioxide elimination and usually respiratory-pump failure or severe ineffective ventilation. Both can coexist.

Respiratory failure is a clinical emergency, not merely a laboratory threshold. Increasing oxygen need, severe work of breathing, inability to speak, altered mental status, cyanosis, exhaustion, hemodynamic instability, a worsening blood gas, or failure to respond to initial support requires rapid escalation.

Obstructive and restrictive patterns fail differently

Obstructive disease increases resistance and limits expiratory flow. Asthma produces variable bronchoconstriction and inflammation; COPD may combine small-airway disease, mucus, and loss of elastic recoil. Prolonged exhalation, wheeze, air trapping, and dynamic hyperinflation can increase work and reduce venous return. Wheeze intensity does not measure severity—a nearly silent chest can be ominous.

Restrictive processes reduce lung expansion or total usable volume. Causes may arise from lung tissue, pleura, chest wall, obesity, pain, or neuromuscular weakness. Rapid shallow breathing can maintain minute ventilation temporarily but may increase the proportion of wasted ventilation and promote fatigue.

ARDS disrupts barrier integrity and lung mechanics

Acute respiratory distress syndrome involves inflammatory injury to the alveolar–capillary barrier, protein-rich edema, surfactant dysfunction, atelectasis, reduced compliance, and severe gas-exchange impairment. The process is not explained by hydrostatic heart failure alone, although cardiac and noncardiac mechanisms can coexist.

Shunt physiology can make hypoxemia difficult to correct with oxygen alone. Management may require treatment of the precipitating cause, lung-protective ventilatory strategies, appropriate positive end-expiratory pressure, positioning, conservative fluid management when clinically appropriate, and close monitoring. These decisions require current orders, protocols, and interprofessional management.

Support the failing step and reassess the whole client

Interventions may include airway positioning, suctioning when indicated, bronchodilation, secretion mobilization, treatment of inflammation or infection, supplemental oxygen, reversal of respiratory-depressant effects, noninvasive support, or invasive ventilation. Positioning can improve mechanics and V/Q matching, but the safest position depends on the disease, hemodynamics, aspiration risk, and tolerance.

Oxygen is a medication: select and titrate the prescribed delivery system to the individualized target and reassess. Excess oxygen can contribute to absorption atelectasis, oxidative injury, or worsening hypercapnia in susceptible clients through several mechanisms; this is not a reason to withhold oxygen from a hypoxemic emergency. Give indicated support while monitoring response.

Positive pressure can recruit alveoli and reduce work of breathing, but may reduce venous return, lower blood pressure, overdistend alveoli, or cause barotrauma. The RN monitors interface and airway safety, synchrony, pressure, respiratory effort, oxygenation, ventilation, mental status, skin, hemodynamics, and evidence of air leak or deterioration.

Improvement means less physiologic strain
A higher SpO₂ is incomplete evidence if the client is more somnolent, breathing more shallowly, retaining CO₂, or becoming hypotensive. Reassess oxygenation, ventilation, effort, mentation, perfusion, and the underlying cause together.

Translate respiratory physiology into clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify airway patency, respiratory rate and depth, work of breathing, chest movement, air entry, sounds, cough, secretions, oxygen device and setting, SpO₂ signal quality, mentation, skin, perfusion, capnography, blood gases, imaging, and trends.
  2. Analyze cues: Organize findings as airway obstruction, increased resistance, low compliance, hypoventilation, V/Q mismatch, shunt, diffusion limitation, impaired oxygen content, or a mixed mechanism.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Obstructed airway, apnea, exhaustion, rapidly worsening oxygenation, acute hypercapnic encephalopathy, tension pneumothorax, massive pulmonary embolism, and severe ARDS outrank stable chronic findings.
  4. Generate solutions: Plan airway and oxygen support, positioning, monitoring, prescribed cause-directed therapy, ventilatory assistance, diagnostic evaluation, and escalation thresholds.
  5. Take action: Stay with the unstable client, activate the appropriate response, support airway and breathing, verify equipment, implement time-sensitive protocols and orders, and communicate the complete trend.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess symptoms, effort, rate and depth, air movement, SpO₂, mental status, capnography or blood gases when indicated, perfusion, device tolerance, and treatment complications.

Clinical example

A client with severe airway obstruction was tachypneic and using accessory muscles. The respiratory rate now falls, breath sounds are barely audible, the client can no longer speak, and alertness is decreasing despite an improved SpO₂ on supplemental oxygen. The RN recognizes impending ventilatory failure rather than improvement. The RN activates emergency escalation, supports the airway and ventilation, continues indicated oxygen, prepares for advanced respiratory support, and evaluates mental status, air movement, hemodynamics, capnography, and blood gases.
